question: What are the principal ways to combine physics knowledge and machine learning for prediction, and which choices govern whether the result solves, identifies or generalizes across physical systems?

key_findings.claim: The survey organizes physics-aware prediction along three intervention points—model, objective and data—and three capabilities—simulation, system inference and cross-system generalization.
key_findings.evidence: Its taxonomy separates differential-equation models, algebraically structured parameterizations, physics-informed losses, neural operators, latent dynamics, system identification, invariances, multi-task/meta-learning and neural processes. Table 1 makes explicit that these families solve different problems despite often sharing the same label.

key_findings.claim: Physics knowledge is an inductive bias whose value depends on calibration, not an automatic guarantee of correctness.
key_findings.evidence: The review argues that domain structure can reduce irrelevant search and improve small-data learning, but overly restrictive assumptions underfit. PINNs additionally face residual optimization, loss balancing, spectral bias and collocation difficulties; structured Hamiltonian/Lagrangian models can suffer numerical instability or miss non-conservative effects.

key_findings.claim: Generalization across boundary conditions and systems motivates operator, multi-task, meta and contextual learning rather than solving every instance from scratch.
key_findings.evidence: Neural operators learn mappings between function spaces; multi-task/meta methods share information across experiments; neural processes condition predictions and uncertainty on contextual measurements. These approaches treat collections of physical instances as data-derived prior knowledge.

key_findings.claim: Industrial adoption is constrained less by isolated benchmark accuracy than by data access, uncertainty, reliability and integration with existing solvers.
key_findings.evidence: The industrial survey spans manufacturing, power, fluids, robotics and process control but notes sparse/confidential data and distrust of opaque models. The conclusion predicts hybrid warm starts rather than wholesale solver replacement and prioritizes uncertainty, simulation-to-real gaps and physics foundation models.

method.core_idea: Provide a machine-learning-centered taxonomy for physics-aware prediction that distinguishes where knowledge enters and what kind of generalization the model must perform.
method.mechanism: Synthesize methods across ODE/PDE modeling, structured networks, residual losses, operator and latent models, identification, invariances, multi-task/meta/contextual learning, then map published industrial uses and open-source tools.
assumptions: Published method descriptions and application reports are sufficiently comparable for a shared taxonomy.
Physics knowledge can be represented as model structure, objective constraints, augmented data or task/context distributions.
Prediction is a useful common scope even when individual fields use different terminology.

techniques.role: Classifies where physical prior knowledge enters learning.
Separates instance solution, system identification and cross-instance learning.
Links method families to reported deployment domains.

evaluations.setting: Literature synthesis across physics-informed prediction methods.
evaluations.metric: Coverage and conceptual differentiation rather than a quantitative meta-analysis.
evaluations.result: A broad taxonomy covers model-, loss-, data- and context-based incorporation of knowledge.
evaluations.baseline: Earlier surveys centered more narrowly on PINNs, operators or architectural priors.

evaluations.metric: Presence of studies across sectors and method categories.
evaluations.result: Examples span aerospace, manufacturing, automotive, energy, fluids, robotics, optics, climate and process control.
evaluations.baseline: The evidence is heterogeneous and is not normalized by readiness level, compute, data or classical-solver performance.

evaluations.metric: Supported methods, backends, geometries and benchmark coverage.
evaluations.result: DeepXDE, Neuromancer, Modulus, SciML, neuraloperator, PDEBench, PDEArena and related projects are summarized.
evaluations.baseline: A time-stamped inventory rather than reproducible package benchmarking.

limitations: As a survey, it does not experimentally rank method families or estimate effect sizes.
Its extremely broad scope makes treatment uneven and terminology across disciplines remains ambiguous.
Industrial examples are publication reports, not independent deployment audits.
Physics consistency at sampled points does not imply global numerical accuracy, robustness or conservation.
Comparisons often lack matched compute, data, mesh resolution and classical-solver baselines.
The open-source appendix and foundation-model landscape age quickly.
The focus on forward prediction leaves inverse design and sensing less developed.
failure_modes: A hard physical bias omits relevant unmodeled dynamics and systematically underfits.
A soft residual loss is numerically small at collocation points yet produces a poor global solution.
A learned surrogate is fast in-distribution but fails under new geometry, boundary conditions or discretization.
Synthetic physics data dominate scarce measurements and create a reality-gap bias.
A model reports point predictions without calibrated uncertainty in safety-critical operation.
reusable_insights: First specify whether the task is solving one system, identifying its law or generalizing across a family.
Compare physics priors at the model, objective, data and inference levels rather than treating PINNs as the whole field.
Benchmark hybrid ML-plus-solver workflows as well as end-to-end replacement.
Physical residual, predictive error, conservation, uncertainty and out-of-domain robustness are separate metrics.
open_questions: Which priors improve out-of-distribution reliability after controlling for data and compute?
How can scientific-ML uncertainty be calibrated under sparse industrial measurements?
When is a learned warm start more cost-effective than a surrogate replacement?
Can physics foundation models transfer across equations, meshes, geometries and regimes without hiding conservation failures?

competitive_landscape.title: When Physics Meets Machine Learning: A Survey of Physics-Informed Machine Learning
competitive_landscape.difference: This survey organizes motivations, representations of physics and integration methods; the reviewed survey adds a solve/infer/generalize distinction, data-as-prior framing and a larger industrial/software perspective.

competitive_landscape.title: Physics-Informed Machine Learning: A Survey on Problems, Methods and Applications
competitive_landscape.difference: Hao et al. classify tasks, prior representations and incorporation mechanisms; the reviewed work emphasizes prediction, multiple-experiment learning and ML-centered deployment choices.

competitive_landscape.title: Scientific Machine Learning through Physics-Informed Neural Networks: Where we are and What's next
competitive_landscape.difference: This review deeply catalogs PINN variants and challenges, whereas the reviewed paper deliberately broadens beyond residual losses to operators, structured dynamics, task distributions and contextual models.

competitive_landscape.title: Operator Learning: Algorithms and Analysis
competitive_landscape.difference: This work provides focused algorithms and theory for function-to-function learning; the reviewed survey positions operator learning among several distinct routes for integrating physics and generalizing across systems.

novelty_assessment: Its primary contribution is integrative: a useful capability-by-intervention taxonomy plus industrial and software context. It is broader than several predecessor surveys, but readers still need specialist reviews and matched benchmarks before choosing a method; coverage should not be mistaken for evidence that physics-informed ML reliably beats classical solvers.
reviewer_notes: Read all 61 pages, including the full taxonomy, method families, practical PINN/operator caveats, industrial discussion, conclusion and open-source appendix. Four primary competing surveys/reviews were checked on 2026-08-23.
